item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports diagnosing history dependence through prediction changes. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) proposes a recency metric and reports that excessive recent-item emphasis harms accuracy across its evaluated models. [TRACE (RecSys 2026)](https://github.com/devUuung/TRACE) uses influence-guided position selection, plausible substitutions and actual ranking margins to find history edits that promote or demote target items. A [2026 temporal-attribution study](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates perturbation explanations through faithfulness, robustness, k-sufficiency and mask-versus-shuffle consistency. These approaches motivate measuring both score margins and ranking changes, rather than interpreting attention weights alone.\n\nFor this diagnostic, a proposed synthesis is to compare deletion and reinsertion of recurrent, isolated and recent events against repeated count- and position-matched random controls. Freeze candidates and the original unseen-item exclusion set; otherwise deleted items becoming eligible can confound ranking changes. Report paired excess effects over controls, with uncertainty, separately by category and event type. Compare position-preserving masking with compacted deletion because shifting positions introduces another intervention. Define lexical recurrence using available titles/descriptions, without assuming it reveals intent. Ablate a lexical residual only if the trained architecture actually exposes that component; compare its contribution before and after each history intervention. This can localize model reliance on sustained versus emerging lexical patterns, but perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish causal effects on user preferences. The complete matched-control protocol is a methodological proposal, not an established result of these papers."}
